examples.label: TCP port scan range (-z = zero-I/O scan mode)

notes: Banner grabbing reveals service version and OS info without authentication — quick fingerprinting before Nmap. `-z` (zero-I/O mode) scans without sending data, useful for fast open/closed detection across a port range. `-w 1` sets a 1s timeout per port. PowerShell `Test-NetConnection` is the Windows equivalent for interactive use; the TCP loop is useful when nmap is unavailable. Try both nc and telnet — some services respond differently. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 6 (Information Gathering).

recommended.note: Full service scan of the host.

name: Netcat - Banner Grab
description: Connect raw to a port to read its service banner - the quickest manual way to fingerprint a service. -n skips DNS, -v is verbose.

defense.why_it_works: Adversaries scan for open ports and running services on network hosts to identify attack surface and potential exploitation targets. Tools like netcat, nmap, and service-specific clients probe for banner information that reveals software versions, which can then be matched against known vulnerabilities.
defense.prerequisites: Network access to the target and a known open TCP port.
defense.impact: The service name and version banner, used to fingerprint the service and match it against known CVEs.
defense.detection: Monitor for processes performing network enumeration by correlating process creation, socket connections, and sequential destination IP probing within a time window. Unusual port scanning patterns or banner-grabbing activity from internal hosts can indicate post-compromise discovery.
defense.artifacts: A TCP connection to the service port in firewall/IDS logs, and a connection entry in the service's own log.
defense.prevention: Close unnecessary ports and services to prevent risk of discovery and potential exploitation. Use network intrusion detection/prevention systems to detect and prevent remote service scans. Ensure proper network segmentation to protect critical servers and devices.
defense.misconfiguration: Common introductory misconfigurations: services running as root/SYSTEM unnecessarily, default credentials unchanged, unnecessary services listening on all interfaces, lack of firewall rules exposing services externally, no monitoring or alerting on authentication failures.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Service listening on all interfaces with default creds (common in labs/staging):
ss -tlnp | grep LISTEN
# 0.0.0.0:21  (FTP on all interfaces)
# 0.0.0.0:3306 (MySQL on all interfaces — should be 127.0.0.1 only)
# 0.0.0.0:8080 (Tomcat with manager app accessible)

# Running services as root:
ps aux | grep -E '(mysql|apache|nginx|ftp)'
# root  1234  /usr/sbin/mysqld  <-- should run as 'mysql' user
defense.secure_config:
# Bind services to localhost or specific IPs (not 0.0.0.0):
# MySQL: my.cnf -> bind-address = 127.0.0.1
# Apache: Listen 127.0.0.1:80 (if behind a proxy)

# Run services as dedicated low-priv users:
# systemd unit: User=mysql Group=mysql

# Host-based firewall (ufw):
ufw default deny incoming
ufw allow from 10.10.1.0/24 to any port 22  # SSH from mgmt only
ufw allow 443  # HTTPS
ufw enable

# Change all default credentials immediately after installation
# Enable fail2ban for SSH and web services
